books.section: Topic 4.6 Market Revolution: Society and Culture, B. The Market Revolution's Impact on Economic Class

stimulus.text:
Population of leading American cities, from the United States census (U.S. Census Bureau, Working Paper 27):

| City | 1800 | 1850 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| New York | 60,515 | 515,547 |
| Philadelphia | 41,220 | 121,376 |
| Baltimore | 26,514 | 169,054 |
| Boston | 24,937 | 136,881 |
stimulus.source_note: U.S. Census Bureau, Working Paper 27, Population of the 100 Largest Cities and Other Urban Places, Tables 3 (1800) and 8 (1850). Figures verified against the Census Bureau tables.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The growth of cities shown in the table went along with which change in American society?

options.text: The end of wage labor and a return to farming
options.misconception: City growth meant more wage labor, not less; farming still employed most Americans, but cities ran on wages.

options.text: The closing of the West to new settlement
options.misconception: The West was opening, not closing; more than four million Americans crossed the Appalachians between 1800 and 1840.

options.text: The growth of a middle class alongside a large laboring poor
The disappearance of religious revivals from city life
options.misconception: Revivals flourished in cities as well as the countryside during the Second Great Awakening.

rationales.A: Cities ran on wage labor: factory hands, dock workers, and servants. Growth meant more wages, not a return to farming.
rationales.B: The same decades saw the West fill with settlers. Cities grew while the West opened, not while it closed.
rationales.C: Cities needed banks, offices, and shops, which made work for clerks, lawyers, and other white-collar workers. At the same time, the poor crowded into the same cities, so growth widened the gap between rich and poor.
rationales.D: The Second Great Awakening filled city churches and revival meetings. Religion did not leave the cities as they grew.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what a growing city needs. Banks, offices, shops, and shipping all need workers.
2. Split those workers in two. White-collar clerks and professionals form a middle class; factory hands and laborers form a laboring poor.
3. Name the change. Cities grew a middle class and a poor class at the same time.
Background: On the eve of the Civil War, about 5 percent of Americans controlled half the country's wealth.
Remember: growth that lifts some people and crowds others is two changes at once.
